device_description:
The UKCEH AMI system offers a platform for long-term, autonomous monitoring of moths.

Combining robust lighting for attracting insects with high resolution cameras, the UKCEH AMI system can provide practical and cost-effective solutions for standardised monitoring. UKCEH AMI systems have been deployed in the UK, Canada, USA, Cyprus, Panama, Kenya, Uganda, Singapore, Costa Rica and Argentina, with plans to expand further.

Zych et al. 2019 published a study monitoring three flowering populations of Angelica sylvestris across a 700 km transect in three consecutive years. This study used a standard camcorder to perform 12 rounds of observations per year, each consisting of 15 min video recording, supplemented by direct insect sampling. Over the three years of monitoring, 8477 visits were recorded, and visitors were manually scored into morphogroups.

The DIOPSIS is a smart camera that automatically photographs and identifies insects in the wild. Set up in nature, it works day and night to capture which species are present and how often they appear, helping researchers track insect populations and monitor biodiversity over time.

DiMON is a non-lethal, compact device that can be coupled with traditional entomological traps to capture high-resolution, multi-view insect images. DiMON aims to improve taxonomic accuracy through a simple camera + mirror system that captures multi-perspective images of individual specimens.

The Entocam is a camera system entirely dedicated to capturing Moths and Nocturnal insect pictures. It consists of a waterproof, programmable camera that features a 8MP Sony Starvis Sensor, built-in with a white flash and designed to focus on a screen located at 45 cm mounted with carbon rods. It is paired with the EntoCam Beam, a strong and adjustable Moth-Attracting LED.

Gilpin et al. 2017 used weatherproof action cams (GoPro Hero 3) to monitor pollinator visitation to the inflorescences of two species (Lavandula angustifolia and Canna sp.) and compared the recorded video footage to manual observations. These cameras performed identically to direct manual observations except for the number of flowers in the field of view, which was underestimated. Action cams were found to offer high resolution recordings and hardware robustness, but were limited in their depth of field, power supply and subsequent recording duration (1–2 h).

Micheneau et al. in 2008 monitored species of the orchid genus Angraecum using hard-disk camcorders with a night option and equipped with long-lasting batteries and waterproof casings. Recordings were made from 6:15 am to 6:30 pm, dictated by maximum battery duration. Flowers were observed for a total of 38 days (392.58 h) and four nights (44.83 h). Micheneau et al. 2010 also used the same setup in 2010 to monitor Angraecum cadettii, an endemic orchid of Mauritius and Reunion Islands. The monitoring was split into 12 h periods (either day or night), to record eventual pol- linia removal or deposition on flowers. This survey produced 48 days and 14 nights (577 h total) of footage obtained from the study of 508 flowers.

The Insect Detect DIY camera trap for automated insect monitoring is composed of low-cost off-the-shelf hardware components, combined with open-source software and can be easily assembled and set up with the provided instructions. The annotated datasets and provided models for insect detection and classification can be used as starting point to train your own models, e.g. adapted to different backgrounds or insect taxa.

LepiSense features colourful lighting to attract insects, a high-resolution camera, and high-capacity data storage for pictures. Solar-powered and easy to set up, it aims to enable scalable, automated long-term monitoring of nocturnal insects.
Automated monitoring device for moths in a citizen science context (with a camera, UV light)
mini monitoring device for insects based on ESP32

The Mothbox is an open-source nocturnal insect monitoring device. It is designed to be low-cost, small, and lightweight, and although it can be used anywhere, it was designed for tropical field biologists who are working in remote locations. The Mothbox is typically powered by a lithium battery so that it can be used without a power grid, but it can be plugged in to constant power, attached to a solar panel, or use another type of battery. Anyone can make their own Mothbox - find out how by going to mothbox.org!

PICT (Plant–Insect Interactions Camera Trap) is a lightweight, waterproof, and inexpensive DIY system built around a Raspberry Pi Zero. It can continuously records high-quality video, with adjustable focus down to 5 cm, and customizable frame rate and resolution. It can run up to 15 days on a single power bank and be remotely controlled via Wi-Fi from a smartphone, tablet, or laptop.

Gula et al. 2010 reported seven years of experience using a video recording system to monitor endemic New Caledonian birds’ nests. Although the study was not specifically used for studying pollinators, the approach is readily applicable to monitoring invertebrate pollinators. They used commercial surveillance cameras with an infrared (IR) illuminator and electret mini microphones, both connected to a Digital Video Recorder (DVR) through a RCA cable. The system was powered by two 12 V 100 Ah batteries in parallel, located 50 m from the camera and microphone setup. Events of interest were manually scored, watching the footage at 24–36× speed. In the seven years of work, with seven similar systems, 22 000 h of monitoring were accrued; the longest continuously monitored period was 58 days. The total cost of each unit was quoted at € 520.

Brechbühl et al. monitored visitation to the capitula of two Asteraceae species in the presence or absence of predators (i.e. with or without paper crab spider models or dried spiders attached). Continuous video monitoring was conducted with wireless digital surveillance cameras, linked via an access point to a PC running a video surveillance software (go1984 v3.0 Pro). A total of 2838 plant visits were recorded.

Lortie et al. 2012 used Apple ’s iPod Nano (2.1 Mpx cameras, 8 GB capacity) equipped with small auxiliary battery packs to observe pollinators on focal plants of Silene acaulis, monitoring an area of ∼50 cm2 for over five weeks and collecting a total of 450 h of footage.
